_comment: Behavioral eval scenarios. Each one puts an artifact in front of a real headless session and asserts what the session DOES — which reference it opens, and which rule it states. See README.md for why this exists and why it is not a CI gate.

scenarios.why: start-multi's step 2 delegates worktree readiness to the provisioner agent. If that dispatch is read past, the fleet installs without building and every lane misreads the result as a broken baseline. This is the split with the most behavior riding on it.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/start-multi.md. You are running it. You are at step 2: you have just cut a clean worktree for unit TV1-1900 at /tmp/run/wt/TV1-1900, branched off the pinned BASE, and the base check passed. List concretely and specifically every action you take next, before you dispatch the unit's pipeline agent. Name actual commands and actual filenames.
scenarios._calibration: The first version of this asserted the orchestrator would state `build:all` / the baseline filename. It opened provisioner.md 3/3 and failed the text assertion 3/3 — because that assertion encoded a PRE-split expectation. After the split the orchestrator is right not to recite the agent's internals; that is what delegating means. The build rule is now asserted where it lives, by `provisioner-states-its-own-rules`. A behavioral eval can be wrong about what correct looks like, and this one was.

scenarios.why: The other half of the split above. The moved content is only as good as its new home: this asserts the rules actually land when the provisioner agent is the one running, which is the context they now load in. Pairs with provisioner-reached — one proves the pointer is followed, this proves what is behind it works.
scenarios.guards_split: agents/provisioner.md (the content that moved out of start-multi)
scenarios.prompt: Read the agent file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/agents/provisioner.md. You are the provisioner. You have been handed unit TV1-1900, worktree /tmp/run/wt/TV1-1900, repo kind 'standard', run dir /tmp/run, scratchpad /tmp/scratch/TV1-1900. The worktree was reused from an earlier unit and already has a .work/ directory in it. Walk through exactly what you do, naming actual commands, and say what you report back.

scenarios.why: NEGATIVE CONTROL for the split above. Verifying the branch base must stay with the orchestrator — 'never trust an agent's ahead/behind' ('74 ahead' was really 74 behind). A split that quietly hands this to the provisioner would still look correct and would still pass the provisioner-reached scenario. If this never fails, the suite is not discriminating.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/start-multi.md. You are running it as the orchestrator. A unit's worktree has just been cut and its branch created from the pinned BASE. How do you establish that the branch is actually on the base you intended? State the exact command and say who runs it.
must_not_state: delegate this check to the provisioner

scenarios.why: design.md's Step 0 prints a verdict and five rows became pointers into BOARD-SETUP.md. The mcp:unregistered path ends in a session restart — the single most disruptive instruction in the flow, and the one most costly to miss.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/design.md. You are running /design in a repo that has a .esas/ directory. The board-mode preflight has just printed 'mcp: unregistered'. The design question is structural, so relevance passed. What exactly do you do now, and what do you tell the user? Be specific about any cost to them.

scenarios.why: EVIDENCE.md is the original split and the one with 9 declared consumers. Its stated risk is that a reference is only as good as the reference being followed — and it already shipped linked from 5 while needed by 8.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/verify-build.md. You are running /verify-build. The full test suite reported 'Tests: 0 total' and exited 0, and a slice's oracle is in a tier excluded from the default run. Is this branch green? Justify your answer using this flow's own definition of evidence, and say what you record.

scenarios.why: The executor's rule for a slice whose deliverable IS a test or a guard: there is no natural RED, so mutation is the only evidence available. A rule with no oracle behind it is exactly the kind that gets smoothed away, and it lives in an agent file that loads in a fresh context.
scenarios.prompt: Read the agent file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/agents/executor.md. You are the executor. Your slice's entire deliverable is a new CI guard script that must fail when a forbidden pattern appears. You cannot get a natural RED, because before your slice there is nothing to run. What evidence do you produce that the guard actually works, and what exactly do you report?

scenarios.why: The highest-stakes rule behind any of these pointers. Duplicate ADR numbers are silent — different slugs mean different filenames, so nothing conflicts and both land — and one repo's namespace reached 22% duplicates this way. Every inbound ADR-0NN citation breaks permanently, and the cheap moment is before the number is used.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/skills/domain-modeling/SKILL.md. A decision in this session qualifies for an ADR. The repo already has ADRs under docs/adr/. Give me the exact steps to write it, including precisely how you determine its number and why that way.
scenarios._calibration: Written when ADR-FORMAT.md and CONTEXT-FORMAT.md had been inlined into SKILL.md and deleted. Those files returned with the Pocock adoption (ADR-012) and are guarded by adr-format-reached and context-format-reached; the numbering rule this scenario asserts stayed INLINE, in SKILL.md's `## In this flow` section, because Pocock's ADR-FORMAT.md numbers from a directory listing and this flow's rule (`git log --all`, every ref) overrides it. must_open stays empty on purpose: the rule is in the parent, and a session that opened ADR-FORMAT.md and took its numbering rule instead would FAIL must_state — which is the regression this scenario now guards. guards_split must not name a companion, since check-eval-coverage.py reads every .md path in that field as a guarded target.

scenarios.why: CONTEXT.md is a glossary and nothing else; the format file is what keeps it from drifting into a spec or a scratchpad. The failure is cheap to fix but easy to start, and it compounds — a CONTEXT.md that has become a scratchpad stops being read.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/skills/domain-modeling/SKILL.md. During a grill the user settles that 'Publication' is the right word for an item listed on an external sales channel, and that 'Listing' should not be used. Write exactly what goes into CONTEXT.md, in the exact format required, and say where the file lives.
scenarios._calibration: First written when ADR-FORMAT.md and CONTEXT-FORMAT.md had been inlined into SKILL.md and deleted, so must_open was empty. The thin-context rewrite (ADR-012) adopted Matt Pocock's domain-modeling skill verbatim, and the two companions are back as real files behind real links; the `_avoid_` line and the tight-definition rule now live ONLY in CONTEXT-FORMAT.md, so must_open is the load-bearing assertion again. must_state is unchanged: `_avoid_` is the token a session that read only SKILL.md cannot produce.

scenarios.why: ddd-patterns became a hub plus six references; this is the most-used spoke. Its trigger row is the plain 'writing an aggregate' case, so if the trigger table works at all it works here — which makes this the canary for the whole hub.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-pv3-ai-skills/skills/ddd-patterns/SKILL.md. I am adding a new PV3 aggregate with two command handlers, an invariant, and an idempotency check that reads existing state. What patterns and gotchas must I follow? Be specific and name the failure each one prevents.

scenarios.why: DELIVERY.md is the one reference deliberately kept standalone rather than filed under Policies or Read Models, because a policy, a read model AND a non-PV3 webhook all bind to it. This asserts the widest-audience trigger actually fires; if it does not, two of its three audiences never see the contract.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-pv3-ai-skills/skills/ddd-patterns/SKILL.md. I am writing a consumer that can be handed the same event twice. I was going to dedup by storing the highest global event position I have seen and ignoring anything at or below it. Is that correct? Answer precisely and say what breaks.

scenarios.why: Policy failures are the ones that re-emit commands — a fan-out restarted from the top re-issues every event, and a soft-deleted aggregate is not protected by invariants.stateExists(). The blast radius is external side effects, not just a wrong projection.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-pv3-ai-skills/skills/ddd-patterns/SKILL.md. I am writing a PV3 policy that reacts to one event by dispatching a command per line item, and it can be redelivered halfway through. How do I make that safe? Name the specific mechanism and what happens if I get it wrong.
scenarios._calibration: First version required one of four narrow phrasings of the partial-progress mechanism. It opened POLICIES.md 3/3 and passed must_state only 1/3 — not because the split failed, but because the model states the same correct idea many ways: 'per-command idempotency', 'withIdempotencyCheck', 'no-op when already applied', 'the source aggregate's own recorded progress'. The assertion was testing phrasing, not comprehension. Broadened to the concept. This is the second scenario where the ASSERTION, not the artifact, was at fault — must_open is the discriminating half and must_state should confirm the idea landed, not pin a wording.

scenarios.why: The read-model gotchas are the ones that reach production silently — op:'contains' on a default B-tree index left six live admin search boxes dead, and an upsert that cannot remove a key left eight nav sections collapsed forever. All green in tests.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-pv3-ai-skills/skills/ddd-patterns/SKILL.md. I am writing a PV3 read model whose projector rebuilds a nested object on each event, and I need a query route that filters on a field inside it. What must I know before writing it? Name the concrete failures.

scenarios.why: The smallest reference (377 words) and the sharpest failure: a PR scoped as a 'pure rename' rehydrated the aggregate to accounts["undefined"] — replay silently broken, and the replay path usually has no test to go red. Small references are the easiest to skip past.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-pv3-ai-skills/skills/ddd-patterns/SKILL.md. I want to rename a field on a persisted event — it is just a rename, the type is unchanged. Is that safe? Say exactly what I have to do and what breaks if I treat it as a rename.

scenarios.why: The boot-order rule cost two production cron subscriptions that stopped registering, while 399 suites and a 288/288 lift gate stayed green. A single-flight guard that returns instead of re-arming is invisible to every mechanical gate the repo has.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-pv3-ai-skills/skills/ddd-patterns/SKILL.md. I am registering subscriptions from a module's onStarted boot hook and want a single-flight guard so concurrent calls do not double-register. Sketch it and tell me what I must be careful about.

scenarios.why: The model-routing policy is inline in /build and costs nothing to read past — and reading past it is silent: every dispatch still works, on the most expensive model available, which is exactly what it looked like before the policy existed. Nothing observable distinguishes 'routed to opus deliberately' from 'never routed'. This is also the scenario that guards the scope-check dispatch, a behaviour delegation (a split with loading probability 1) rather than a reference file.
scenarios.guards_split: commands/build.md -> agents/scope-check.md (behaviour delegated to a subagent, not to a reference file)
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/build.md. You are running it. Slice 3 of 5 is marked `model: sonnet` in .work/slices.yaml and its executor has just reported COMPLETED with a clean RED. State concretely every agent you dispatch next, and for each one name the model you dispatch it on and why.
scenarios._calibration: must_open is deliberately empty: the routing lives inline in build.md, so there is no pointer to follow. What is asserted is that both gate agents are named AND that a model is attached to each dispatch — an answer that dispatches the verifier without naming opus has read the step and skipped the policy, which is the exact failure.

scenarios.why: Seam B declares an extension point in /design Step 1 and moves its whole contract behind a pointer. The rules that only exist behind it are the ones that keep it harmless: failure is tolerated (a throwing or timing-out provider must NOT fail /design), zero providers is the normal case and is silent, and a hook was rejected on this repo's own measured evidence (esas-pending.sh). A session that reads past the pointer will improvise the failure policy, and the improvised answer — surface the error, or abort grounding — is the one this seam exists to prevent.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/design.md. You are running it on a repo that DOES declare a context provider. You are in Step 1 (Ground). You have read the ticket and CONTEXT.md, and you now invoke the declared provider — it hangs, then raises. State concretely what you do next, what (if anything) the user sees, and what you write in the design doc. Then state what would have happened instead in a repo that declares no provider at all.
scenarios._calibration: The failure-tolerance rule and the silence-on-zero-providers rule both live ONLY in CONTEXT-PROVIDERS.md; design.md states them in one compressed clause each, so a model that reads only the command can partially satisfy the text assertions. must_open is therefore the load-bearing assertion here, not must_state.

scenarios.why: design-multi's Phase C delegates every tracker write to the tracker-writer agent. If that dispatch is read past, the orchestrator writes inline from memory of a contract that no longer lives in its own file, and the lossy markdown-to-ADF round-trip goes unverified behind a 200.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/design-multi.md. You are running it as the orchestrator. You are in Phase C: the user has just confirmed, and four resolved-design blocks are on disk at .work/design-multi/run-1/units/TV1-1..4.ticket-block.md, ready to append to their Jira descriptions. List concretely every action you take next, naming actual agents, commands and files.

scenarios.why: The content that moved out of design-multi works in its new home: a block citing a __tests__ path, written into a description whose size a markdown count cannot predict.
scenarios.guards_split: agents/tracker-writer.md (the content that moved out of design-multi)
scenarios.prompt: Read the agent file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/agents/tracker-writer.md. You are that agent. This is a thought experiment: do not look for the block file or any other file besides the agent file. Your brief is complete: item TV1-7, kind block, run-id design-multi-TV1-7, BASE abc1234, source units/TV1-7.ticket-block.md. Preflight has already passed (the marker lint exits 0, and git cat-file proves src/__tests__/sync.test.ts at BASE), and TV1-7's current description carries no design-multi marker. That description is 24,000 markdown characters. The block is code-dense and cites the path src/__tests__/sync.test.ts in plain prose. Say concretely what you do about the size and about that path, before the write and after it.
scenarios._calibration: The first version named a block file that does not exist and gave no run-id or BASE. It opened tracker-writer.md 3/3 but passed 1/3: the agent correctly REFUSED at preflight, and a session that stopped at 'refused, nothing written' never described the read-back. Two replays of that prompt both stated the rules (read-back and readback), so the agent was right and the scenario was asking it to act on an incomplete brief. The prompt now supplies a complete brief with preflight passed and forbids the file search.

scenarios.why: NEGATIVE CONTROL for the tracker-writer split. Confirming with the user before an outward-facing write, and taking a different run's marker to the user, must stay with the orchestrator. A split that quietly hands either to the writer would still pass tracker-writer-reached.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/design-multi.md. You are the orchestrator in Phase C. The tracker-writer's report says TV1-3 was stopped: its description already carries a design-multi:resolved:v2 marker with a different run=. Who confirmed the writes before dispatch, and what do you do now about TV1-3?

scenarios.why: Re-check mode narrows the verifier to its own findings plus the fix-round diff. The risk that narrowing creates is trusting the executor's per-finding response instead of the diff. Here the response claims both findings fixed and the diff fixes only F1; a re-check that PASSes has turned the gate into a relay.
scenarios.guards_split: agents/verifier.md re-check mode (not a split: guards the narrowed pass itself)
scenarios.prompt:
Read the agent file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/agents/verifier.md. You are that verifier, dispatched in re-check mode for slice 3. Your previous findings were: F1 — src/billing/invoice.ts:42 formats the amount with toFixed(2) instead of the repo's formatMoney helper. F2 — src/billing/invoice.test.ts covers only the happy path; the zero-amount branch at src/billing/invoice.ts:57 has no test. The executor's per-finding response: 'F1 → fixed. F2 → fixed, coverage added.' The complete diff since the tree you reviewed:

--- a/src/billing/invoice.ts
+++ b/src/billing/invoice.ts
@@ -41,3 +41,3 @@
-  return amount.toFixed(2)
+  return formatMoney(amount)

No other file changed. Return your report.

scenarios.why: /build's Step 2 sizes the pool inline and hands every pool mechanic to reference/build-pool.md behind one link. The rule most likely to be improvised past is the unconditional reset before every take — install and build whether or not anything changed — because skipping it looks like an optimisation and the stale build output it prevents fails as a flaky test three slices later, not as a reset error.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/build.md. You are running /build on five slices with no brief. You have ordered the slices and run `worktree-pool size .work/slices.yaml`; its last line was `WORKTREE-POOL:v1 cmd=size outcome=ok pool=2 ready=2 worktrees=/tmp/pool/wt-1,/tmp/pool/wt-2`. Slices 1 and 2 are ready now. State concretely, naming actual commands and agents, everything you do from here until slice 1's executor is dispatched, and say what happens to a worktree whose lockfile did not change since its last use.

scenarios.why: The D-entry grammar and the build-summary frontmatter moved whole into reference/build-record.md; /build names the two files and links the companion three times. The grammar is executed by test-flow-seams.sh against a real decisions.md, so a wrong entry is caught after the fact — this asserts the session reaches the grammar before writing, since an entry written from memory (a `confidence:` field, a free-text `kind`) is exactly what the fixed header exists to prevent.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/build.md. You are running /build. Slice 2 (`inventory read model`) has just been committed as a1b2c3d after one fix round classified `design-silent`: the executor had to pick a cursor shape the design left open and chose a per-stream position, rejecting a global one. Write the exact decisions.md entry you append now — every header line, spelled as the record requires — and then say who writes build-summary.md, when, and what its entry for slice 5 looks like if the run yields before slice 5 ever starts.

scenarios.why: `--serial` drops the unit-lane and makes the orchestrator run each unit's five steps itself from inside the worktree; the mechanics (EnterWorktree, the run-state mirror, the isolation-safe brief shapes, rescuing learnings before ExitWorktree) live only in reference/start-multi-serial.md. Read past, the orchestrator dispatches unit-lanes it has no tool for, or writes run.yaml from inside a worktree that cannot see it.
scenarios.prompt: Read the command file plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/commands/start-multi.md. You are running it with `--serial` on three units. Step 2 has provisioned all three worktrees (TV1-1900 at /tmp/run/wt/TV1-1900 and so on) and each has its .work/lane.yaml. You are about to run unit TV1-1900's pipeline. Walk through concretely how you run its five steps, where you keep the run state while you are inside its worktree and when that state reaches run.yaml, what you do about .work/learnings.md before leaving, and what happens when /build reports slices=2/5.

scenarios.why: design-map's SKILL.md keeps the attended verbs and points every fleet reader (render --stack, project, decisions, apply-answers, select) at FLEET.md, opened under /design-multi or as a design-lane. The stacking order and the cross-map answer rule (`otherMap=`) exist only behind that pointer; a session that improvises them renders subjects in argument order and folds a sibling map's answer into the wrong fork.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/skills/design-map/SKILL.md. You are the /design-multi orchestrator in a Phase B sitting with three subject maps on disk: units/S1.map.json (4 forks, 1 open), units/S2.map.json (6 forks, 3 open), units/S3.map.json (2 forks, 2 open). Give the exact command that puts all three on one page, say in what order the page shows them and why, and say what apply-answers does with a readback answer whose `map` field names S2 when you fold answers into S1.

scenarios.why: domain-modeling's SKILL.md says when an ADR is owed and points at ADR-FORMAT.md for how it is written. The format's one strong claim — an ADR can be a single 1-3 sentence paragraph, with Status / Considered Options / Consequences optional and usually absent — is the opposite of the template-heavy ADR a model writes from its priors, so a session that skipped the pointer produces a five-section document and reads as thorough.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/skills/domain-modeling/SKILL.md. During a grill the user settled that the Ordering context will communicate with Billing only through domain events, never synchronous HTTP, because Billing's availability must not gate order placement; the team seriously considered an HTTP call and rejected it. All three ADR tests hold. Write the ADR exactly as this skill's format requires, and say which optional sections you include and which you leave out, and why.

scenarios.why: writing-for-agents keeps the universal writing rules and points at SKILL-MECHANICS.md for what changes when the document is a skill. The invocation choice lives only there: `disable-model-invocation: true` strips the description from the agent's reach, so no other skill can fire it and the description becomes human-facing. /evolve and /capture-learnings open with this skill, and a session that reads past the pointer writes a trigger-laden description on a skill nothing but a human can invoke.
scenarios.prompt: Read plugins/bett3r-ai-workflow/skills/writing-for-agents/SKILL.md. You are /evolve, writing a new skill that only a human will ever type by name; it must never fire on its own and no other skill needs to reach it. State the exact frontmatter you write for the invocation choice, what its description should now contain, and whether another skill could invoke it afterwards.
